messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 27
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Taxi/Uber Driver
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event, Auditory (Footsteps): Footsteps behind or nearby, Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others, Distraction: I distract myself with something else, Drug Use: take drugs
  Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kofi is a 27-year-old man of Ghanaian descent who drives for a rideshare company in a mid-sized American city. He came to therapy at the urging of his cousin, who had noticed that Kofi had stopped coming to family gatherings and seemed increasingly isolated and on edge. Kofi himself was not sure what he hoped for, only that he was exhausted.

The event that shaped his life happened when he was nine years old, living with his father in the Bronx. His father, a man Kofi described as hardworking and strict, had a particular way of disciplining him that involved making Kofi kneel on a cold linoleum floor for hours, sometimes with his hands pressed flat against the icy tile. The punishment was always preceded by the sound of footsteps—heavy, deliberate, approaching from behind—and then the cold would spread up through his palms and knees until his whole body felt locked in place. He remembered the texture of the linoleum: a slightly raised, bumpy pattern that pressed into his skin and left temporary indentations. His father would stand behind him, silent, and the temperature of the floor would seep into him, and he would feel his body contract as if trying to disappear.

Now, as an adult, Kofi lives alone in a small apartment. He works long shifts, often driving late into the night, and he has come to believe that he is permanently changed for the worse. He says it quietly, without self-pity: “I’m not the same person. Something broke in me back then, and it never healed.” He is certain that his body has become his enemy. Even when he is safe—sitting in his parked car, or lying in bed—his heart will suddenly pound, his skin will prickle, and he will feel that old cold spreading across his palms. He knows intellectually that no one is coming, but his body does not believe it. He has tried to explain this to people, but they tell him he is safe now, and he finds it impossible to believe them. Their words feel like a foreign language.

The triggers are everywhere, woven into the fabric of his daily life. When he picks up a passenger and the seatbelt buckle has a certain bumpy texture, his hand jerks back. When he hears footsteps behind him on the sidewalk—especially if they are heavy and steady—his shoulders lock and he has to fight the urge to sprint. And the temperature: he cannot stand cold floors. He wears slippers constantly, even in summer. He has removed the bathmat from his bathroom because the texture of it reminded him of something he cannot name, and he now steps onto a towel instead.

To manage this, Kofi has developed a set of strategies that have slowly hollowed out his life. He avoids intimacy completely. He has not dated in years, and he has stopped responding to friends who try to get close. He is afraid that if someone touches him, or if he lets himself feel attached, the old cold will come back, or worse, he will snap at them or push them away. So he stays alone. When the memories press in during his shifts, he distracts himself by turning the radio up loud, or by focusing obsessively on the road, or by counting license plates. And sometimes, when the pressure is unbearable, he smokes marijuana in his car between rides. He tells himself it helps him sleep, but he knows it also helps him not feel.

The consequences have been concrete. He has lost his connection to his community. His church used to be a central part of his life—the Ghanaian congregation, the shared meals, the elders who knew his family—but he stopped going two years ago. He cannot bear the thought of being surrounded by people, of being seen, of having to explain why he flinches when someone claps him on the back. He has also become reckless. He drives too fast sometimes, especially at night, weaving through traffic, taking risks that he knows could get him in trouble. He is not trying to hurt himself, exactly, but he is not trying to stay safe either. He is hypervigilant in a way that exhausts him: scanning every rearview mirror, checking every sound, always watching for footsteps that are not there.

What finally brought Kofi to seek help was a moment in his car last month. He had picked up a passenger who, after getting in, reached forward to adjust the air conditioning. The cold air hit Kofi’s hand, and for a second he was nine years old again, kneeling on that floor. He pulled the car over, told the passenger to get out, and sat shaking for twenty minutes. That night, he called his cousin. He is not sure if therapy can help, but he knows he cannot keep living like this. What he is most afraid of is that he is right—that he really is permanently damaged, and that no amount of talking will change the cold that lives under his skin. But he is also afraid of staying the same.
